name: Agents and their Impacts (Wind & Running Water)

notes.heading: Geomorphic Agents – Overview
points: Agents like wind and running water shape landforms
Impact depends on climate, slope, and rock type
Running water is the most dominant agent
Wind is dominant in arid regions

notes.heading: Wind – Overview
points: Important agent in arid and semi-arid regions
Carries fine particles like sand and dust

notes.heading: Comparison: Wind vs Running Water
points: Water is more powerful than wind
Water acts in all climates, wind mainly in deserts
Water carries all sizes of sediments, wind mainly fine particles
Wind forms smaller but distinct features

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Rivers form deltas
2. Wind forms dunes
3. Water is more powerful than wind

name: Agents and their Impacts (Groundwater, Glaciers, Waves & Currents)

notes.heading: Geomorphic Agents – Extended Overview
points: Groundwater, glaciers, waves and currents are important geomorphic agents
Operate through erosion, transportation and deposition
Each agent is dominant in specific environments

notes.heading: Glaciers – Overview
points: Dominant in polar and high mountain regions

notes.heading: Waves & Currents – Overview
points: Driven by wind and ocean currents
Cause erosion and deposition along coasts

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Groundwater forms caves
2. Glaciers form moraines
3. Waves form beaches

name: Winds as Agents in Hot Deserts (Deflation, Abrasion, Impact & Erosional Landforms)

notes.heading: Wind as a Geomorphic Agent (Hot Deserts)
points: Wind is the dominant geomorphic agent in hot desert regions
Works effectively where vegetation is sparse
Transports fine sand and dust particles

notes.heading: Processes of Wind Erosion – Overview
points: Wind erodes surface through three main processes

notes.heading: Deflation
points: Removal of loose particles by wind

notes.heading: Erosional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed mainly by deflation and abrasion
Unique shapes due to wind action

notes.heading: Pediments and Pediplains
points: Pediment – gently sloping rock surface at mountain base
Formed by erosion and retreat of slopes
Pediplain – large plain formed by merging pediments

notes.heading: Playas
points: Dry lake beds most of the time

notes.heading: Deflation Hollows and Caves
points: Depressions formed by removal of sand

notes.heading: Mushroom, Table & Pedestal Rocks
points: Lower part erodes faster due to sand impact

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Deflation removes particles
2. Abrasion polishes rocks
3. Playas are dry lakes

notes.heading: Wind Depositional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed when wind loses energy and deposits sand
Common in deserts and semi-arid regions
Shape depends on wind direction and sand supply

notes.heading: Barchans (Crescent Dunes)
points: Form in areas with limited sand supply
Horn-shaped ends point in wind direction

notes.heading: Seif Dunes (Longitudinal Dunes)
points: Form parallel to prevailing wind direction
Develop in areas with two wind directions

notes.heading: Parabolic Dunes
points: Horns point opposite to wind direction

notes.heading: Transverse Dunes
points: Ridges of sand perpendicular to wind direction
Form in areas with abundant sand

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Barchans are crescent-shaped
2. Seif dunes are longitudinal
3. Parabolic dunes are vegetation anchored
Parabolic dunes differ from barchans because:

notes.heading: Running Water – Overview
points: Most important geomorphic agent on Earth
Shapes valleys, plains, and drainage systems

notes.heading: Erosional Processes by Rivers
points: Hydraulic action – force of moving water
Abrasion – scraping of bed and banks

notes.heading: Rills
points: Very small channels formed by running water

notes.heading: Valleys – Overview
points: Shape depends on rock type and stage of river

notes.heading: V-Shaped Valleys
points: Formed in upper course of river

notes.heading: Gorge
points: Deep, narrow valley with steep sides
Formed in hard and resistant rocks
Very deep compared to V-shaped valley

notes.heading: Canyon
points: Less steep than gorge but wider

basic.question: Running water is the most important:

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Rills are smallest erosion features
2. Gullies form from rills
3. Valleys are final stage

name: Potholes, Plunge Pools, Incised Meanders & River Terraces

notes.heading: River Erosional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed mainly in the upper and middle course of rivers
Developed due to strong erosional activity
Controlled by slope, velocity and rock type

notes.heading: Potholes
points: Circular depressions formed on river bed
Created by swirling pebbles and sediments

notes.heading: Plunge Pools
points: Deep depressions at the base of waterfalls
Form due to falling water impact

notes.heading: Difference: Potholes vs Plunge Pools
points: Plunge pools → formed by falling water impact
Potholes are smaller and shallow initially
Plunge pools are deeper and associated with waterfalls

notes.heading: Incised (Entrenched) Meanders – Overview
points: Form due to vertical erosion of river
Indicates uplift of land or rejuvenation

notes.heading: Types of Incised Meanders
points: Form due to change in base level

notes.heading: River Terraces – Overview
points: Step-like landforms along river valley sides

notes.heading: Paired River Terraces
points: Occur at same level on both sides of river

notes.heading: Unpaired River Terraces
points: Occur at different levels on opposite sides
Form due to lateral erosion or uneven uplift

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Potholes are formed by abrasion
2. Plunge pools form at waterfalls
3. Terraces show river evolution

notes.heading: River Depositional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed when river loses energy and deposits sediments
Common in middle and lower course of rivers
Depends on velocity, gradient, and sediment load
Creates fertile plains and coastal features

notes.heading: Alluvial Fans
points: Cone-shaped deposits at foothills of mountains
Form where river suddenly loses slope and velocity
Often found in arid and semi-arid regions

notes.heading: Delta
points: Triangular or fan-shaped deposit at river mouth
Formed where river meets sea or lake

notes.heading: Types of Deltas
points: Control by waves, tides, river load

notes.heading: Natural Levees
points: Coarser sediments near channel, finer away

notes.heading: Point Bars
points: Depositional features on inner bends of meanders
Form due to lower velocity of water

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Alluvial fans form in piedmont zones
2. Deltas form at river mouths
3. Floodplains are fertile
Which statement is correct?
options: Alluvial fans form at river mouth

notes.heading: Meanders – Overview
points: S-shaped bends in a river course
Form in mature stage of river

notes.heading: Formation of Meanders
points: Water flows faster on outer bend
Water flows slower on inner bend

notes.heading: Slip-off Slope (Point Bar)
points: Formed on inner bend of meander

notes.heading: Undercut Bank (Cut Bank)
points: Formed on outer bend of meander

notes.heading: Oxbow Lake – Overview
points: U-shaped water body formed from abandoned meander
Occurs when river cuts through neck of meander

notes.heading: Formation of Oxbow Lake
points: Flood or erosion cuts through neck

notes.heading: Braided Channels – Overview
points: Occurs in high sediment load areas
Common in mountain and glacial rivers

notes.heading: Difference: Meandering vs Braided Rivers
points: Meanders form in low sediment areas
Braided rivers form in high sediment areas

moderate.question: Oxbow lake is formed due to:

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Slip-off slope is depositional
2. Cut bank is erosional
3. Oxbow lake forms from meander cut-off
Which statement is correct?
options: Meanders form in high slope areas

name: Groundwater (Karst Topography – Permeability, Percolation, Bedding Plains)

notes.heading: Groundwater – Overview
points: Water present below Earth's surface in soil and rocks
Major agent in karst landform development

notes.heading: Karst Topography – Overview
points: Landforms formed by dissolution of soluble rocks

notes.heading: Permeable Rocks
points: Rocks that allow water to pass through pores or cracks

notes.heading: Impermeable vs Permeable Rocks
points: Karst develops only in permeable soluble rocks

notes.heading: Percolation
points: Downward movement of water through soil and rock
Leads to cave formation in limestone areas 🔥

notes.heading: Bedding Plains
points: Act as pathways for groundwater flow
Facilitate development of caves and joints
Important structural control in karst regions

notes.heading: Role in Karst Formation
points: Leads to caves and sinkholes formation

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Permeable rocks allow groundwater flow
2. Percolation helps in cave formation
3. Bedding planes guide water movement
Karst landforms are mainly formed by:

notes.heading: Karst Region – Overview
points: Karst topography is well developed in Balkan and Adriatic regions
Named after Karst Plateau in Slovenia

notes.heading: Swallow Hole
points: Natural opening where surface water disappears underground
Acts as entry point to underground drainage

notes.heading: Uvalas (Valley Sinks)
points: Large depressions formed by merging of sinkholes

notes.heading: Lapies (Karren)
points: Small grooves and furrows on limestone surface

notes.heading: Limestone Pavements
points: Cut by deep cracks called grikes

basic.question: Karst region is mainly found in:

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Sinkholes form in limestone regions
2. Uvalas are larger than dolines
3. Lapies are early stage karst features

name: Karst Caves and Depositional Landforms (Stalactites etc.)

notes.heading: Karst Caves – Overview
points: Underground hollow spaces formed in soluble rocks
Formed by dissolution of rock by groundwater

notes.heading: Role of Different Rocks in Cave Formation
points: Shale – weak permeability, limited cave formation
Sandstone – forms caves through erosion and seepage
Quartzite – very hard, caves rare and limited
Rock type controls cave development significantly

notes.heading: Formation of Caves
points: Groundwater percolates through cracks and joints
Expands fractures into tunnels and chambers

notes.heading: Depositional Landforms in Caves – Overview
points: Formed due to precipitation of dissolved minerals
Occurs when water loses CO₂ inside caves

notes.heading: Stalactites
points: Hanging icicle-shaped deposits from cave roof
Form due to dripping water rich in minerals

notes.heading: Pillars (Columns)
points: Form when stalactites and stalagmites join

notes.heading: Process of Deposition in Caves
points: Water enters cave carrying dissolved CaCO₃

moderate.question: Tunnels in caves are formed due to:

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Caves are formed by groundwater action
2. Stalactites hang from roof
3. Pillars form when stalactite and stalagmite meet
Sandstone caves are formed mainly by:

notes.heading: Stalagmites – Overview
points: Depositional landforms formed inside limestone caves
Created by dripping water rich in calcium carbonate

notes.heading: Formation of Stalagmites
points: Water drops fall from cave roof

notes.heading: Characteristics of Stalagmites
points: Generally broader and shorter than stalactites

notes.heading: Mnemonic Tip
points: So they grow from the ground upward

notes.heading: Pillar Columns – Overview
points: Created when stalactite and stalagmite meet
Extend from cave roof to floor

moderate.question: Both stalactites and stalagmites are made of:

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Stalagmites form on cave floors
2. Pillar columns form by joining of stalactite and stalagmite
3. Both are formed by chemical deposition
Which statement is correct?
options: Pillars are formed by water erosion

notes.heading: Glaciers – Overview
points: Form in cold regions above snowline
Create distinct erosional and depositional landforms

notes.heading: Cirque (Corrie)
points: Formed at the head of a glacier
Created by glacial plucking and abrasion
Steep back wall and hollow basin

notes.heading: Tarn Lake
points: Lake formed in a cirque after glacier melts

notes.heading: Horns
points: Formed by erosion from multiple cirques
Several glaciers erode a mountain from different sides

notes.heading: Arêtes
points: Form between two cirques or valleys

notes.heading: Fiords (Fjords)
points: Form when glacial valleys are flooded by sea
Steep valley walls and deep water

notes.heading: Sequence of Glacial Erosion
points: Arêtes and horns form at ridges

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Cirques are glacial birthplaces
2. Tarn lakes form in cirques
3. Fiords are submerged glacial valleys
Which statement is correct?
options: Horn is formed by river erosion

advanced.question: Tarn lakes are formed due to:

notes.heading: Glacial Depositional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed by deposition of sediments carried by glaciers
Material ranges from fine clay to large boulders
Occurs mainly during melting or stagnation of ice

notes.heading: Glacial Till
points: Unsorted mixture of sediments deposited directly by ice
Includes clay, sand, gravel, and boulders

notes.heading: Moraines – Overview
points: Can be found at sides, front, or underneath glacier

notes.heading: Types of Moraines
points: Lateral Moraine – along sides of glacier
Medial Moraine – formed when two glaciers merge
Terminal Moraine – at glacier end (maximum advance)

notes.heading: Eskers
points: Long, winding ridges of sand and gravel
Formed by meltwater streams under glaciers

notes.heading: Outwash Plains
points: Broad, flat plains in front of glaciers

notes.heading: Drumlins
points: Steep side faces glacier origin, gentle slope opposite

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. Till is unsorted material
2. Eskers are formed by meltwater streams
3. Drumlins indicate ice movement direction

name: Waves and Currents (High Rocky Coasts & Low Sedimentary Coasts)

notes.heading: Waves and Currents – Overview
points: Together they create diverse coastal landforms

notes.heading: Wave Action – Basic Concept
points: Generated by wind blowing over sea surface

notes.heading: Currents – Role in Coasts
points: Longshore currents move sediments parallel to coast
Help in redistribution of sand and silt
Responsible for deposition features like spits

notes.heading: High Rocky Coasts – Overview
points: Example: Western coast of India (Konkan cliffs)

notes.heading: Features of High Rocky Coasts
points: Sea cliffs – steep vertical rock faces

notes.heading: Formation of Sea Cliffs and Platforms
points: Wave erosion at base of rock

notes.heading: Low Sedimentary Coasts – Overview
points: Made of loose sediments (sand, silt, clay)

notes.heading: Features of Low Sedimentary Coasts
points: Beaches – accumulation of sand and pebbles
Bars – submerged ridges parallel to coast

notes.heading: High Rocky vs Low Sedimentary Coasts
points: High energy vs low energy environment

advanced.question:
Consider the following:
1. High rocky coasts are erosional
2. Low sedimentary coasts are depositional
3. Waves are primary coastal agents

notes.heading: Coastal Erosional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed by continuous wave action on coastlines
Lead to development of steep and rugged coastlines

notes.heading: Cliffs
points: Steep or vertical rock faces along coast
Formed by wave erosion at base of landmass
Wave cuts a notch → overhang collapses
Common in hard rock coasts (granite, basalt)

notes.heading: Wave-cut Notch (Key Step)
points: Formed at base of coastal cliff
Leads to instability of upper part

notes.heading: Caves
points: Hollow cavities formed in coastal rocks
Develop along weak zones or joints
Waves force air and water into cracks

notes.heading: Stacks
points: Formed after collapse of sea arches

basic.question: Coastal cliffs are formed mainly by:

notes.heading: Coastal Depositional Landforms – Overview
points: Formed by deposition of sediments by waves and currents
Occurs mainly in low-energy coastal environments
Sediments include sand, silt, and pebbles
Shaped by longshore drift and wave action

notes.heading: Beaches
points: Gently sloping accumulation of sand or pebbles
Formed by wave deposition along shoreline
Constantly reshaped by tides and waves

notes.heading: Types of Beaches
points: Each depends on wave energy and material supply

notes.heading: Coastal Dunes
points: Formed by aeolian deposition of beach sand
Act as natural barriers against sea intrusion
Common in arid and coastal regions

notes.heading: Bars
points: Submerged or emerged ridges of sand

notes.heading: Barriers (Barrier Islands)
points: Long narrow sandy islands parallel to coast
Separated from mainland by lagoon or bay
Formed by wave and current deposition
Protect coast from strong wave action

notes.heading: Spits
points: Narrow extension of sand projecting into sea or lagoon
Curved tip often due to wave refraction
Can evolve into bars or barriers

notes.heading: Bars vs Spits vs Barriers
points: Bar → ridge parallel or across coast
Barrier → offshore island separated by lagoon

notes.heading: Weathering – Context
points: Weathering is controlled not only by rocks and climate
Topography and vegetation also strongly influence it
These factors modify intensity and type of weathering

notes.heading: Topographic Factors – Overview
points: Relate to relief, slope, and elevation
Control drainage, exposure, and erosion intensity
Steepness is a key controlling factor

notes.heading: Slope (Most Important Topographic Factor)
points: Steep slopes → faster removal of weathered material
Steep areas expose fresh rock surfaces continuously

notes.heading: Relief and Elevation
points: High relief areas have intense physical weathering
Low relief areas favor soil accumulation
Higher altitude → lower temperature → freeze-thaw action

notes.heading: Drainage and Runoff
points: Rapid runoff increases erosion and exposure

notes.heading: Vegetative Factors – Overview
points: Acts as protective layer on rocks
Important in biological and chemical weathering

notes.heading: Role of Vegetation Cover
points: Roots penetrate rocks causing mechanical breakdown
Protects soil from direct rainfall impact

notes.heading: Vegetation vs Bare Surfaces
points: Vegetated areas → slower erosion but more chemical activity
Forests show slow but deep chemical alteration

notes.heading: Interaction of Factors
points: Vegetation controls protection and chemical activity
Both modify climatic and geological effects
